name: PCDH19-related epilepsy
aliases: epilepsy in females with mental retardation

reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in the X-linked PCDH19 gene, with an unusual inheritance in which heterozygous females are affected while hemizygous males are typically unaffected carriers
Seizures usually begin in the first years of life, often triggered by fever, and characteristically occur in tight clusters over hours to days
Focal seizures with prominent fear or affective features are common during clusters
Development ranges from normal to intellectual disability, and autistic and behavioural features may emerge
Seizure clusters tend to become less frequent with age, and many patients improve markedly by later childhood
The condition can resemble Dravet syndrome, but SCN1A testing is negative and PCDH19 testing is diagnostic
Management focuses on aggressive treatment of clusters and fever control, sometimes with steroid or benzodiazepine strategies during acute clustering
reference.pathophysiology: PCDH19-related epilepsy arises from variants in the X-linked PCDH19 gene, which encodes protocadherin-19, a cell-adhesion molecule involved in neuronal migration and network formation. The unusual sex-limited pattern is explained by cellular interference: random X-inactivation in heterozygous females produces a mosaic of cells with and without functional protocadherin-19, disrupting cell-cell communication, whereas hemizygous males express a uniform population and are usually spared. This mosaic disruption of neuronal connectivity underlies the fever-sensitive seizure clusters and the associated cognitive and behavioural features.
additionalDifferentials: Genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+)
additionalInvestigations: PCDH19 gene testing, often within an epilepsy panel, especially in girls with clustering fever-related seizures
SCN1A testing to distinguish from Dravet syndrome
EEG during and between clusters, which may be normal or show focal/generalised discharges
Brain MRI to exclude structural causes
redFlags: Prolonged seizure clusters progressing to status epilepticus
New developmental regression or behavioural deterioration during a cluster
Fever-triggered clustering in a young girl resembling Dravet syndrome
Marked affective or fear semiology raising diagnostic uncertainty
reference.prognosis: Seizure clusters are often severe in early childhood but frequently diminish or remit with age, so the epilepsy prognosis is generally more favourable than in Dravet syndrome. Cognitive and behavioural outcomes vary widely, from normal development to significant intellectual disability and autistic features.
pitfalls: Assuming Dravet syndrome and stopping after a negative SCN1A result without testing PCDH19
Overlooking the diagnosis in an affected girl with an apparently unaffected carrier father
Underestimating the intensity of acute clusters and undertreating them
Attributing behavioural features solely to epilepsy rather than the underlying disorder
